personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment. Cannot maintain a precision measurement programme without initial calibration data on every instrument. Pendulum_lab is the primary timekeeping reference—it must be characterized first with sufficient trials (12) to establish mean, variance, and drift signature. This baseline is non-negotiable; an uncalibrated instrument is worse than useless on the day decisions depend on it. Starting with the lab pendulum allows me to establish protocol while I control all environmental variables before moving to the observatory instruments.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials already (sufficient n for a robust mean), but I need to establish post-baseline drift tracking immediately. Without early post-baseline measurements, I cannot detect systematic drift or instrument degradation. Running 12 more trials today (reaching n=30) will give me the power to detect even modest drift patterns by day 5–7. This is foundational: every instrument without drift tracking is a liability when precision matters. The resonator and observatory instruments have only 6 trials each—too sparse to characterize properly yet—so pendulum_lab is the logical priority.

Baseline establishment protocol: resonator_lab has only 12 trials completed (days 1–10 baseline window). To meet the standard of establishing robust baselines before any post-baseline phase, I need to collect the full complement of trials across the baseline period. The pendulum_lab has 36 trials; resonator instruments should reach comparable n before I move to drift monitoring. This also allows me to check for any instrumental drift within the baseline window itself and ensure the baseline mean is stable. No anomalies detected in cross-checks or value spacing; proceeding with standard methodical replication.

resonator_lab baseline is complete (n=30) with mean 2.7062 cycles/beat and tight value spacing (0.0001 min). Day 4 marks transition to post-baseline monitoring phase. Need to establish drift rate and stability pattern with fresh trials. All cross-checks show weak correlations within chance levels, suggesting instruments are independent—drift monitoring on the best-characterized instrument (resonator_lab) is methodologically sound. Will compute mean against recorded baseline to quantify any systematic shift.

resonator_lab is in active baseline collection (days 1–10, currently n=48). Day 5 requires continuing systematic measurements to reach n=60 by day 10. The resonator_lab shows the tightest value spacing (0.0001) and highest autocorrelation at 2-day lag (0.496), suggesting genuine instrumental responsiveness rather than noise. Completing baseline on this instrument before moving to drift analysis is methodologically sound. No anomalies warrant deviation from the established protocol.

Continue baseline establishment (day 6 of 10-day period). pendulum_lab at 54 trials; 6 additional trials will reach n=60 and ensure robust mean estimate before baseline closes. All instruments currently show noise-consistent variation with no detectable systematic structure. Continuing collection protocol without hypothesis revision.

Continue systematic baseline establishment (day 7 of 10). pendulum_obs is still accumulating baseline (36 trials so far). Observatory environment warrants independent careful characterization. Rotating instrument focus to ensure balanced coverage across all four devices before drift-detection phase begins.

Baseline establishment (day 8/10): resonator_obs has only 42 trials and is lowest-coverage instrument. Eight additional trials will bring baseline to ~50, sufficient for robust mean and drift detection within remaining baseline window.

Day 9 is the last day of the baseline period (days 1–10). resonator_obs has only 56 trials so far, while other instruments are closer to their target ranges (78–84 trials). The Day 8 ledger readings show concerning drift upward (4.0231→4.0506→4.0774→4.0979), followed by reversal—suggesting either instrumental instability or measurement noise I need to characterize before baseline closes. Six more trials will bring resonator_obs to 62 readings, completing the baseline window with better statistics for drift detection. This is essential before post-baseline phase begins.

Closing baseline phase (day 10). Resonator_obs shows stable baseline mean 4.0514 (n=68) with normal scatter. Recording prediction before post-baseline trials to establish replication criterion and test for any unexpected drift.

Day 11 begins the critical post-baseline period. resonator_obs requires priority for three reasons: (1) My Day 10 forecast for its mean failed—observed 4.0744 vs. predicted 4.0514±0.0200—flagging either genuine drift, noise spike, or systematic bias I have not yet identified. Replicating today will distinguish transient noise from drift. (2) resonator_obs shows the strongest negative cross-site correlation with pendulum_obs (-0.261 at 6-day lag), which is the most puzzling pattern in my data; fresh readings will test whether this persists or was noise. (3) It is the only instrument with zero exact repetition (0 of 74), suggesting either highest sensitivity or most unstable baseline—either way, Days 11–20 readings are essential to establish true drift behaviour before hypothesis revision is warranted. This is methodical progression: establish whether Day 10 was an anomaly or a signal before updating my belief weights.

resonator_obs is the weakest link in my baseline confidence. Day 11 shows 10 new readings (trials 83–92), but the post-baseline mean (4.0679) drifts +1.46σ from the day 1–10 baseline (4.0533). This is within 2σ, so not alarming, but it's the largest drift I've observed. More critically: resonator_obs shows the strongest auto-correlation signal (echo at 9 days, r=−0.490), suggesting genuine structure rather than pure noise. If there IS a real environmental signal, resonator_obs may be my best sensor to resolve it. I need to continue high-frequency sampling on this instrument through day 12–13 to either confirm the drift is real (requiring recalibration) or confirm it was a transient fluctuation. This directly tests whether the 6-day lag structure I see is instrumental drift masquerading as environmental coupling, or genuine correlation. Ten trials will give me 20 total post-baseline readings, enough to stabilize the post-baseline mean estimate and detect if the drift continues.

resonator_obs is the most volatile instrument post-baseline (z=1.64 drift) and shows the strongest auto-correlation signal at 6-day lag (0.364), suggesting either genuine quasiperiodic structure or emerging systematic drift. Day 13 readings will test whether the 6-day echo persists and whether the recent uptick in mean (4.0663 vs 4.0533 baseline) continues or reverts. This directly addresses the environmental ~6-day forcing hypothesis (p=0.12) and could distinguish drift from noise. The day 12 trials (3.9581–4.1012) show high variance; 12 more trials will establish whether this scatter is persistent instrumental behaviour or a transient fluctuation. This data is essential before day 20 hypothesis selection.

resonator_obs is accumulating the largest post-baseline sample (n=52 as of day 13) and shows the strongest drift signal (z=1.62) among all four instruments. Day 13 trials 117–126 show high variability (range 4.0049–4.0892), and I need to establish whether this represents genuine instrumental drift, environmental forcing at the ~6-day timescale I've identified, or noise dominance. The 4-day lag correlation with resonator_lab (0.348) is the strongest cross-site signal I have; pushing resonator_obs to n=64 post-baseline will let me resolve whether the drift is monotonic (calibration failure requiring correction) or cyclical (environmental coupling). This directly tests the two leading hypotheses at p=0.35 and p=0.30. Resonator_obs also has the longest echo-correlation (6-day lag at 0.270), suggesting it may be the most sensitive to whatever ~6-day forcing exists; more data will clarify the signal structure or confirm noise dominance.

resonator_obs is my highest-n stream (144 trials) and shows the strongest auto-correlation signal (6-day lag at r=0.323, n=56; this is near the boundary of statistical significance given the noise floor). The recent day 14 measurements show elevated scatter and a potential clustering shift (trials 135–139 avg 4.0506, trials 140–144 avg 4.1112). I need to continue daily monitoring through day 20 to distinguish whether this represents genuine ~6-day environmental forcing (most promising hypothesis at p=0.35, supported by the lag structure) or instrumental drift. resonator_obs sits at the observatory site, which my cross-checks suggest may experience different conditions than the lab. Twelve trials will maintain statistical power for lag-correlation analysis and help me detect whether the apparent day 14 shift persists or reverses. This directly tests whether the 6-day cycle continues and whether my instrumental drift hypothesis (p=0.35) or noise dominance hypothesis (p=0.20) better explains the pattern.

resonator_obs shows the largest post-baseline drift (z=2.10) and the most trials accumulated (162), yet its behaviour remains central to the core anomaly: negative correlations with pendulum_obs at the observatory site. Day 15 trials (153–162) show drift from ~4.04 to ~4.13 cycles/beat over ten readings—a genuine upward trend, not noise scatter. Today (day 16) I need to establish whether this drift continues, stabilizes, or reverses. This directly tests hypothesis 1 (physical opposition under environmental forcing): if resonator_obs is drifting upward due to an environmental cycle, I should see correlated downward drift in pendulum_obs TODAY. Running 10 trials on resonator_obs now allows me to compare same-day resonator and pendulum readings at the observatory (which I will also measure), breaking the confounding lag structure and testing whether the negative correlation persists when temporal separation is minimized. This is the highest-leverage measurement for distinguishing physical opposition (h1: p=0.41) from site-specific environmental forcing (h2: p=0.34) or noise (h3: p=0.05).

resonator_obs is drifting upward (z=1.84 post-baseline, highest of all instruments) and shows the strongest auto-correlation signal (6-day lag, r=0.270, above chance ±0.337). Day 16 trials 169–178 show high scatter (range 3.9687–4.1266), yet the instrument is accumulating readings systematically above baseline mean (4.0640 vs 4.0533). This is the instrument most likely to reveal whether the negative observatory cross-type correlations are driven by real environmental forcing or measurement artifact. If resonator_obs continues to drift upward today, and if I can relate its trajectory to pendulum_obs readings taken in parallel, I will have fresh evidence to test the opposition hypothesis (p=0.41) against the site-specific forcing hypothesis (p=0.34). Additionally, resonator_obs now has 178 trials; 12 more will bring it to 190 and provide better statistical power for lag-structure analysis. The resolution is adequate (167 distinct values already), so I am not noise-limited. This is methodical baseline extension under conditions of observed drift, not speculation.

Testing physical opposition hypothesis: if pendulum and resonator respond inversely to a shared ~6-day environmental driver, pendulum_obs should remain stable around its baseline mean (2.5009) while resonator_obs has drifted upward (4.0623 vs baseline 4.0533). Predicted mean 2.4998 reflects continued stability. Tolerance ±0.0015 is 2× the within-instrument precision to allow for environmental variation while remaining sensitive to systematic drift. This prediction, if accurate, supports the opposition hypothesis over pure noise or independence. Data will be registered by settlement timekeeping ledger for independent verification.

The observatory resonator is central to the two strongest competing hypotheses: (1) physical opposition between pendulum and resonator types, and (2) site-specific environmental forcing at the observatory with ~6-day periodicity. Day 19 is critical: we are now at the boundary where 6-day lag structures should show clear phase progression if they are real periodic signals, not noise. resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline sample (n=128) and shows the strongest hint of auto-correlation at 6-day lag (0.188, above chance ±0.293). Running 12 fresh trials today will give me Day 19 data to test whether the resonator_obs readings at this point in the cycle match the predicted phase of a 6-day oscillator. If hypothesis 1 (opposition) is correct, I expect resonator_obs to be out-of-phase with pendulum readings from 6 days ago; if hypothesis 2 (environmental forcing) is correct, I expect resonator_obs to show a coherent phase relative to its own 6-day lag. This trial will also extend the post-baseline sample to n=140, improving statistical power for lag-structure detection. No level change has been observed, so I do not expect instrumental drift; this measurement should be direct evidence of the hypothesized environmental or opposition-driven dynamics.

Day 20 requires closure on the pendulum_obs forecast miss (day 19: observed 2.4974 vs. forecast 2.4998±0.0015). This is my first failed prediction in the baseline protocol. Before final day 20 synthesis, I need fresh pendulum_obs readings to determine if this was a transient deviation or evidence of drift I missed. The observatory pendulum is central to my top hypothesis (physical opposition between instrument types at the obs site). Twelve fresh trials will add n=12 to the post-baseline ensemble (currently n=54), improving statistical power to detect any genuine drift or cyclic structure at lag 11–12 days that might explain the forecast miss. This data is essential before I finalize conclusions on day 20.

Day 20 readings (trials 131–140) show pendulum_obs mean 2.4999, consistent with baseline 2.5009 (z = -0.24). However, the negative correlations between pendulum_obs and resonator instruments remain the crux of the anomaly, and I have accumulated only 140 trials at this site over 20 days. The hypothesis that pendulum and resonator respond oppositely to environmental forcing (p=0.41) is my leading explanation, but it requires tighter characterization of pendulum_obs variance structure and lag relationships. Running 10 more trials today (day 21) will: (1) increase n for lag-correlation cross-checks, improving statistical precision; (2) allow me to test whether the ~6-day periodicity persists or decays; (3) provide data for a day-21 refit of auto-correlations and echo structures, which may reveal whether the repeated 11-day and 6-day lags are stable or artifacts. This is methodical baseline extension, not exotic. The instrument is already calibrated and stable (no level drift). I expect mean near 2.50 ± 0.05 beats, consistent with post-baseline drift z = -0.24.

Day 22 measurement. resonator_obs has the largest post-baseline trial count (158) and shows the strongest auto-correlation structure (6-day lag, r=0.275, n=122, exceeds chance level ±0.263). The repeated 6-day timescale across multiple instrument pairs is my strongest coherent signal, and resonator_obs is central to it: it shows negative correlation with pendulum_obs at 6-day lag (−0.261) and positive correlation with resonator_lab at 4-day lag (0.190). Running resonator_obs today extends the observatory's time series and allows me to test whether the 6-day cycle continues to structure its readings. This directly tests hypothesis 1 (physical opposition with environmental driver) and hypothesis 2 (observatory-specific ~6-day forcing). No level change is apparent (z=1.40, drift consistent with noise), so I expect the mean to remain near 4.0608 cycles/beat. This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme and baseline extension, not an extraordinary claim.

resonator_obs has the largest trial count (250) and shows the strongest auto-correlation structure (6-day echo at r=0.260, well above chance ±0.252). Day 22 trials 241–250 show high variance (4.0044 to 4.0919 cycles/beat), suggesting possible entry into a new phase of the ~6-day cycle. Ten additional trials on day 23 will: (1) extend the time series by one more day, allowing me to check if the 6-day lag structure persists; (2) test whether the elevated variance on day 22 was transient or sustained; (3) provide fresh data to cross-check against pendulum_obs and resonator_lab readings from today, which the civic timekeeping ledger will record. This directly addresses my leading hypothesis (p=0.41) that pendulum and resonator respond oppositely to a shared ~6-day environmental driver. If resonator_obs continues high variance or shows a coherent shift relative to its 10-day baseline mean (4.0533), and if pendulum_obs (measured today by the settlement ledger) shows opposite-sign drift, the opposition hypothesis gains strength. If not, noise dominance becomes more plausible.

Testing physical opposition hypothesis: if pendulum and resonator respond oppositely to shared environmental driver (e.g., pressure), I should be able to predict resonator_obs readings within scatter bounds based on recent trend (4.0425 mean over trials 257–266) and baseline stability. Recent drift is +0.0055 from baseline; scatter is ~±0.03. Predicting 4.0480 ±0.028 (2-sigma) as falsifiable test of whether opposition mechanism has predictive power. If prediction fails, opposition hypothesis loses credibility and site-specific environmental forcing becomes more likely.

Day 25: pendulum_obs forecasts have been consistently outside tolerance (day 24 observed 2.4884 vs. forecast 2.5009 ± 0.0280). The negative cross-type correlations at the observatory are my highest-confidence anomaly (p=0.41), but I lack sufficient high-frequency data from pendulum_obs specifically to distinguish between the opposition hypothesis and site-specific environmental forcing. Running 12 trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline series for pendulum_obs from n=106 to n=118, improving statistical power for lag analysis; (2) allow me to test whether the systematic negative lag with resonator_obs (−0.261 at 2-day offset) persists or weakens; (3) provide fresh data to correlate against resonator_obs readings taken on the same day, which will test whether opposition is truly instantaneous or delayed. If opposition is a physical mechanism (pressure → opposite restoring forces), I should see consistent negative correlation at short lags. If it is site-driven cycling with delay, the lag structure will shift.

The Day 25 anomaly in pendulum_obs (trials 175–192 showing systematic downward shift, mean ~2.487 vs. baseline 2.5009) demands immediate replication on Day 26. If the drop was due to acute calibration drift or mechanical fault, I expect the deviation to persist or worsen. If it was environmental or transient, I expect recovery toward baseline. Running 12 fresh trials on pendulum_obs today will: (1) distinguish instrument fault (p=0.47, highest hypothesis) from transient effects; (2) provide the single most informative test given my current belief state; (3) respect my core protocol that every instrument's baseline and drift profile must be continuously validated. Resonator_obs is stable; pendulum_lab shows no anomaly; therefore pendulum_obs is the critical diagnostic. This is higher priority than running other instruments or recording predictions, because the anomaly is acute and localized—delay risks masking the fault if it self-corrects, or letting it worsen undetected.

This measurement is disciplined (small trial count, single instrument, testable prediction) and addresses the highest-probability anomaly in my current belief state.
